WSGTIM.tuners_guide: Flattening or steepening this curve directly adjusts turbocharger spool response and transient boost ramp-in. Conversely, ramping the boost target upward gently over 0.5 to 1.0 seconds can significantly improve front-wheel-drive traction in lower gears and reduce torque steer on high-horsepower street builds. Because the boost target selection is a running minimum, any point in WSGTIM that is lower than WSGRPM will hold boost down until the timer advances.

* **Minimum-Wins Limitation**: * Evaluated as the second table in `GetBoostTargetFromTables`; lower values will restrict the boost target calculated from `WSGRPM`.
* **Timer Incrementing Dependency**: * `Timer_BoostTimer` increments only while engine speed exceeds `RPMBST` (T1) or `T2RPMBST` (T2).

WSGCLT.overview: WSGCLT establishes the maximum allowable turbocharger boost pressure as a function of engine coolant temperature. Cold engine operating conditions place severe thermal and mechanical stresses on cast iron cylinder blocks, aluminum pistons, and head gaskets, while thick engine oil limits hydrodynamic bearing protection at high turbocharger shaft speeds. To safeguard mechanical components, the controller looks up the coolant temperature and restricts boost to wastegate spring pressure or low levels until the engine warms up to normal operating temperatures above 140 to 160 degF.

Cold engine operating conditions place severe thermal and mechanical stresses on cast iron cylinder blocks, aluminum pistons, and head gaskets, while thick engine oil limits hydrodynamic bearing protection at high turbocharger shaft speeds. To safeguard mechanical components, the controller looks up the coolant temperature and restricts boost to wastegate spring pressure or low levels until the engine warms up to normal operating temperatures above 140 to 160 degF.
WSGCLT.tuners_guide: Raising the cold temperature entries allows the turbocharger to build higher boost before the engine reaches full thermostat operating temperature, but doing so increases the likelihood of mechanical stress or premature head gasket fatigue on cold cylinder walls. The recommended practice is to keep the cold regions of this table clamped to base mechanical boost (typically 5 to 7 psi) below 140 degF, tapering smoothly into full target boost between 160 and 190 degF. If the table includes high-temperature breakpoints above 220 degF, lower those entries to automatically pull boost down and protect the engine if the cooling system begins to overheat.
WSGCLT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Cold Engine Protection**: * Restricts boost targets when coolant temperature is low to protect cold pistons, rings, and turbo bearings. * Clamping entries below 140 degF to base wastegate spring boost prevents cold-engine hammering.
* **Warm-Up Transition**: * Blend boost progressively from 140 degF to 180 degF to deliver full power only once oil and coolant are thoroughly warmed.
* **Overheat Safety Limiting**: * Lowering entries above 220 degF provides built-in thermal protection, de-rating boost if the engine begins running hot.
* **Minimum-Wins Integration**: * If any entry in `WSGCLT` is lower than `WSGRPM`, the controller enforces the lower coolant-based limit in `Temp4`.

WSGCHG.overview: WSGCHG regulates maximum allowable turbocharger boost pressure according to intake manifold charge air temperature. Highly compressed intake air heats up significantly, and if intercooler heat soak or elevated ambient summer temperatures drive charge temperatures excessively high, cylinder knock and pre-ignition risks multiply dramatically. The engine controller continuously samples the charge temperature sensor and uses this table to scale back the boost target if intake air temperatures exceed safe thermal thresholds, preventing knock before ignition retard must intervene.

WSGCHG.tuners_guide: For vehicles equipped with highly efficient aftermarket front-mount intercoolers, this table can be raised across typical operating temperature ranges to sustain full boost during back-to-back pulls. However, retaining a conservative boost reduction at very hot intake temperatures (voltage readings corresponding to temperatures exceeding 130 to 150 degF) provides an indispensable safety layer against bad fuel or severe heat soak in staging lanes. If converting to an intake air temperature sensor with different calibration curves, ensure this table is adjusted to align with the sensor voltage scaling.

* **Charge Temperature Protection**: * Scales boost target downward when intake manifold air temperatures become excessively hot. * Prevents high-load detonation caused by hot compressed air and intercooler thermal saturation.
* **Intercooler Upgrade Tuning**: * Vehicles with large, efficient intercoolers can maintain full boost across wider temperature spans. * Keep a sharp reduction above 140 to 160 degF to guard against bad fuel or hot summer ambient conditions.
* **Sensor Voltage Scaling**: * Table x-axis is indexed by charge temperature sensor voltage (0.0 to 5.0 Volts; lower voltage represents hotter air on NTC thermistors).
* **Minimum-Wins Priority**: * Enforces the lower value into `Temp4` whenever high intake temperature calls for boost de-rating.

MXSBST.overview: MXSBST defines the upper boundary for allowable turbocharger boost pressure as a function of road vehicle speed. Because turbocharged front-wheel-drive vehicles easily break traction and induce severe wheel spin or torque steer in first and second gears, Chrysler engineers incorporated speed-dependent boost limits into the controller. At low vehicle speeds (such as 0 to 25 mph), the table can limit boost to moderate levels, smoothly elevating the ceiling to full boost as vehicle speed climbs and available tire grip increases at higher speeds.

Because turbocharged front-wheel-drive vehicles easily break traction and induce severe wheel spin or torque steer in first and second gears, Chrysler engineers incorporated speed-dependent boost limits into the controller. At low vehicle speeds (such as 0 to 25 mph), the table can limit boost to moderate levels, smoothly elevating the ceiling to full boost as vehicle speed climbs and available tire grip increases at higher speeds.
MXSBST.tuners_guide: Functions as a simple and effective boost-by-speed traction management tool. On high-horsepower street cars running street radial tires, lowering the low-speed table entries (0 to 30 mph) to 7 to 10 psi prevents blown-off front tires upon initial launch and roll-ons, while ramping to 18 to 25 psi above 50 mph when aerodynamics and vehicle inertia provide sufficient tire loading. On dedicated drag cars equipped with slicks and a prepped surface where immediate maximum launch traction is available, tuners set all points in this table to maximum target boost to ensure no speed-based restriction impedes acceleration.
MXSBST.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Boost-by-Speed Traction Control**: * Restricts boost in low-speed operating regions to control wheelspin in 1st and 2nd gears on front-wheel-drive platforms. * Ramp boost progressively from 8 psi at 0 to 20 mph up to full target boost above 50 mph.
* **Drag Racing Configuration**: * If running slicks on a prepped track, max out all table entries (set to 29.4 psi) to ensure immediate full boost in every gear.
* **Speed Sensor Scaling**: * Road speed input is derived from the transmission distance sensor (`VehicleSpeed_HB`); ensure speed sensor calibration is accurate.
* **Running Minimum Priority**: * Evaluated as the fifth table in `GetBoostTargetFromTables`; lower values will clamp `Temp4` downward.

WSGPRT.overview: WSGPRT controls the maximum allowable turbocharger boost target under part-throttle operating conditions based on throttle position sensor voltage. When cruising at partial throttle openings, allowing the turbocharger to build full manifold boost against a partially closed throttle plate can create unpleasant compressor surge, jerky driveability, and excessive intake air heating. If the throttle is not wide open, the controller references this table to ensure boost scales proportionally with accelerator pedal angle, reserving full target boost exclusively for heavy or wide-open throttle demands.
WSGPRT.overview_markdown: `WSGPRT` controls the maximum allowable turbocharger boost target under part-throttle operating conditions based on throttle position sensor voltage. When cruising at partial throttle openings, allowing the turbocharger to build full manifold boost against a partially closed throttle plate can create unpleasant compressor surge, jerky driveability, and excessive intake air heating. If the throttle is not wide open, the controller references this table to ensure boost scales proportionally with accelerator pedal angle, reserving full target boost exclusively for heavy or wide-open throttle demands.
WSGPRT.tuners_guide: Smoothing and reshaping this curve directly refines part-throttle driveability and highway cruising manners. Raising this table increases low-throttle throttle response and mid-pedal acceleration, making the vehicle feel significantly more responsive and eager on passing maneuvers without requiring a downshift. However, raising it excessively at light pedal angles (below 2.0 to 2.5 volts) can make the car twitchy and prone to building unwanted boost on steady highway grades, hurting fuel economy. At wide-open throttle, the controller checks the full-throttle flag and skips this table entirely.
WSGPRT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Part-Throttle Boost Scaling**: * Matches boost ceiling to accelerator pedal position, preventing full boost against a partially closed throttle blade. * Eliminates compressor surge and violent bucking during partial-throttle acceleration.
* **Pedal Responsiveness Tuning**: * Elevating mid-pedal points (2.5 to 3.5 Volts) gives a strong, torquey passing response without needing to floor the accelerator. * Keeping low-pedal points (below 2.0 Volts) at base vacuum/zero boost preserves highway fuel economy.
* **Wide-Open Throttle Bypass**: * At WOT (`b4f_FullThrottle` set), the controller completely skips this table, allowing full boost from `WSGRPM`.
* **Throttle Voltage Baseline**: * Indexed by TPS voltage minus closed-throttle minimum (`TpsVolts - MINTHR_LowestSessionTPS`).
WSGPRT.operating_conditions:

DCWOT.overview: DCWOT provides the open-loop base wastegate solenoid duty cycle curve as a function of target boost pressure for T1 wastegate control. In Chrysler T1 bleed-style wastegate plumbing, the solenoid bleeds pressurized air away from the wastegate actuator canister; higher duty cycle bleeds more pressure to hold the wastegate valve closed and raise boost, while lower duty cycle vents less air, forcing the actuator open to lower boost. The engine controller looks up this base duty cycle from target boost as the foundational starting point for closed-loop regulation, scaled so that 200 counts represents 100 percent duty cycle.

DCWADJ.overview: DCWADJ supplies an engine-speed-dependent signed duty cycle adjustment to the base wastegate duty cycle in T1 control. Turbocharger volumetric flow characteristics and exhaust backpressure shift considerably between low engine speeds and redline; smaller turbine housings often create rising exhaust backpressure that blows the wastegate valve open at high RPM, while larger turbines may build boost progressively. DCWADJ.tuners_guide: Modifying DCWADJ corrects for RPM-related boost sag or boost creep. If boost tails off at high RPM (such as between 5000 and 6200 RPM) as exhaust backpressure pushes against the internal wastegate flapper, increasing the duty cycle adjustment at high engine speeds adds solenoid bleed to hold the gate closed and maintain target boost. If boost creeps higher at high RPM due to port flow limitations, subtracting duty cycle at high RPM reduces solenoid bleed to allow the gate to open further. In stock 2.5L calibrations, this table is often set flat with zero adjustment.

* **Shared Clamping Helper**: * Resulting sum in `Temp4` is clamped to 0 to 200 counts (0 to 100 percent) via `WGDC_AdjustWGDutyCycle`.

MAPPT2.overview: MAPPT2 establishes the minimum manifold gauge pressure threshold that must be reached before the engine controller activates electronic wastegate duty cycle calculations. Below this threshold, manifold pressure is near or below atmospheric pressure, where modulating the wastegate solenoid is unnecessary and would cause needless solenoid wear and clicking. When manifold pressure is below atmospheric pressure plus MAPPT2, the controller zeros the wastegate duty cycle and clears all knock-reduction duty cycle offsets. In factory calibrations, this is set to 15 counts (approximately 1.7 psi of boost).

RPMBST.overview: RPMBST defines the minimum engine speed threshold required to advance the boost ramp countdown timer (Timer_BoostTimer) in T1 wastegate control. The boost ramp timer indexes the time-based allowed boost table (WSGTIM), allowing boost to ramp upward from base spring pressure to full target boost over a calibrated duration. To ensure that the boost timer does not prematurely advance while the engine is lugging at low RPM where the turbo cannot generate full boost, the controller requires engine speed to exceed `RPMBST` before incrementing the timer.
RPMBST.tuners_guide: Setting RPMBST properly ensures that boost ramping occurs only when the engine is operating in an RPM band capable of spooling the turbocharger. DCRPML.overview: DCRPML sets the lower engine speed threshold below which adaptive wastegate duty cycle learning is completely inhibited. At low engine speeds, exhaust mass flow is insufficient to spool the turbocharger to full boost, creating an unavoidable physical underboost condition. If the controller attempted to adapt duty cycle at low RPM, it would erroneously wind the adaptive cells up to maximum. DCRPML locks out adaptive learning below this RPM threshold, ensuring that the controller only adapts in engine operating regions where target boost is physically achievable. Shared between T1 and T2 control routines.
DCRPML.overview_markdown: `DCRPML` sets the lower engine speed threshold below which adaptive wastegate duty cycle learning is completely inhibited. At low engine speeds, exhaust mass flow is insufficient to spool the turbocharger to full boost, creating an unavoidable physical underboost condition. If the controller attempted to adapt duty cycle at low RPM, it would erroneously wind the adaptive cells up to maximum. `DCRPML` locks out adaptive learning below this RPM threshold, ensuring that the controller only adapts in engine operating regions where target boost is physically achievable. Shared between T1 and T2 control routines.
DCRPML.tuners_guide: Defines the low-RPM boundary for closed-loop adaptive learning. In factory calibrations, DCRPML is set to 84 counts (approximately 2688 RPM). When using a small, rapid-spooling stock turbocharger, DCRPML can remain at factory levels or be lowered slightly to 2200 to 2400 RPM. When upgrading to a large aftermarket turbocharger that does not achieve full boost until 3500 to 4000 RPM, DCRPML must be raised to match the new spool RPM. Failing to raise DCRPML on a large turbo will cause the adaptive cells to learn maximum positive duty cycle at low RPM, producing severe boost overshoot once the turbo finally spools.
DCRPML.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Low-RPM Adaptive Lockout**: * Inhibits adaptive wastegate learning below this engine speed to avoid learning during natural turbo spool lag. * Factory setting is 84 counts (approximately 2688 RPM).
* **Large Turbo Upgrades**: * Elevate `DCRPML` to match the real spool-up RPM of large turbochargers (e.g. 3500 to 4000 RPM) to prevent adaptive cell corruption.
* **Stock Turbo Response**: * Small factory Mitsubishi or Garrett T3 turbos can lower `DCRPML` to 2200 to 2400 RPM for earlier closed-loop trimming.
* **Shared Code Usage**: * Enforces low-RPM lockout in both `CalcWGDutyCycleT1` (line 9715) and `CalcWGDutyCycleT2` (line 9988).

DCRPMH.overview: DCRPMH defines the upper engine speed threshold above which adaptive wastegate duty cycle learning is completely inhibited in T2 control. At high engine speeds approaching redline, exhaust gas pulsation and rapid changes in volumetric efficiency can introduce noise into closed-loop boost calculations. DCRPMH establishes an upper RPM boundary to freeze adaptive cell learning, ensuring that the controller relies on established feed-forward baseline tables and prevents high-RPM transients from corrupting learned adaptive trims.
DCRPMH.overview_markdown: `DCRPMH` defines the upper engine speed threshold above which adaptive wastegate duty cycle learning is completely inhibited in T2 control. DCRPMH.tuners_guide: Establishes the upper cutoff for closed-loop adaptive learning in T2 mode. In factory calibrations, DCRPMH is configured to 188 counts (approximately 6016 RPM). If tuning a high-performance engine that revs beyond 6500 or 7000 RPM where adaptive learning is desired up to higher engine speeds, DCRPMH can be elevated to match the extended rev limit. Setting DCRPMH below the primary operating band disables high-RPM adaptive learning entirely, forcing the controller to operate strictly from base open-loop tables at high engine speeds.
DCRPMH.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **High-RPM Adaptive Lockout**: * Engine speed threshold above which adaptive wastegate cell learning is frozen. * Factory setting is 188 counts (approximately 6016 RPM in template, 79 counts / 2528 RPM in legacy calibrations).

* **Freezing Adaptives on Dyno**: * Setting `DCRPMH` low locks out adaptive learning, allowing tuners to dial in open-loop base tables without adaptive interference.

TPSLIM.overview: TPSLIM defines the minimum throttle position sensor delta voltage above idle required to permit adaptive wastegate duty cycle incrementing in T1 control. Adaptive duty cycle learning is designed to calibrate wide-open and heavy-throttle wastegate operation. At light to moderate throttle openings, the throttle blade restricts airflow, making target boost unattainable. TPSLIM prevents the controller from attempting to adapt duty cycle upward unless the accelerator pedal is pressed beyond this calibrated throttle threshold.
TPSLIM.overview_markdown: `TPSLIM` defines the minimum throttle position sensor delta voltage above idle required to permit adaptive wastegate duty cycle incrementing in T1 control. Adaptive duty cycle learning is designed to calibrate wide-open and heavy-throttle wastegate operation. At light to moderate throttle openings, the throttle blade restricts airflow, making target boost unattainable. `TPSLIM` prevents the controller from attempting to adapt duty cycle upward unless the accelerator pedal is pressed beyond this calibrated throttle threshold.
TPSLIM.tuners_guide: Ensures that adaptive boost learning occurs only under genuine high-throttle demands. In factory calibrations, TPSLIM is set to 112 counts, representing approximately 2.2 volts above minimum idle throttle position. Setting TPSLIM too low allows the controller to adapt duty cycle upward during partial-throttle driving, which corrupts the wide-open throttle adaptive grid and causes boost spiking upon full throttle application. Setting TPSLIM higher (such as 3.0 to 3.5 volts above idle) ensures that adaptive duty cycle learning occurs exclusively during heavy throttle pulls.
TPSLIM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Throttle Gating for Adaptive Incrementing**: * Minimum TPS voltage above idle required to permit adaptive duty cycle increases. * Factory setting is 112 counts (approximately 2.2 Volts above session minimum TPS).
* **Preventing Part-Throttle Corruption**: * Prevents the controller from adding duty cycle when throttle is only partially open and airflow is throttled.
* **Heavy Throttle Lockout**: * Raising `TPSLIM` to 3.0 to 3.5 Volts above idle restricts adaptive learning exclusively to wide-open throttle pulls.
* **T1-Specific Architecture**: * Gated exclusively within the T1 adaptive increment routine (`WGDC_IncrementWGAdaptive`).

MAPPT.overview: MAPPT sets the manifold gauge pressure switch point that divides low-load adaptive wastegate learning from high-load RPM-split adaptive learning in T1 control. In Chrysler's 5-cell adaptive wastegate architecture, Cell 1 handles boost levels below MAPPT across all engine speeds. Once target boost exceeds barometric pressure plus MAPPT, the controller switches into Cells 2 through 5, which are partitioned by engine speed. In factory calibrations, MAPPT is set to 68 counts (approximately 7.8 psi of boost).
MAPPT.overview_markdown: `MAPPT` sets the manifold gauge pressure switch point that divides low-load adaptive wastegate learning from high-load RPM-split adaptive learning in T1 control. In Chrysler's 5-cell adaptive wastegate architecture, Cell 1 handles boost levels below `MAPPT` across all engine speeds. Once target boost exceeds barometric pressure plus `MAPPT`, the controller switches into Cells 2 through 5, which are partitioned by engine speed. In factory calibrations, `MAPPT` is set to 68 counts (approximately 7.8 psi of boost).
MAPPT.tuners_guide: When tuning for higher boost targets, MAPPT should be positioned near or slightly above mechanical wastegate spring pressure. If MAPPT is set too low (e.g., below base actuator spring pressure), the controller will prematurely place low-speed spooling into the RPM-split high-load cells. If set too high (e.g., above target boost), the controller will operate exclusively in Cell 1 and never utilize the RPM-dependent adaptive cells (Cells 2 through 5). When upgrading to a 3-bar MAP sensor, MAPPT must be rescaled to match the expanded pressure range.
MAPPT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Adaptive Cell Switch Point**: * Boost threshold dividing low-load Cell 1 from RPM-split high-load Cells 2 through 5. * Factory setting is 68 counts (approximately 7.8 psi boost above atmospheric pressure).
* **Positioning Relative to Spring Pressure**: * Set `MAPPT` 1 to 2 psi above mechanical wastegate spring pressure so low-load spooling stays in Cell 1.
* **3-Bar MAP Sensor Rescaling**: * When converting to a 3-bar MAP sensor, divide count value by approximately 1.5 to maintain proper physical psi switching.

INCPT.overview: INCPT specifies the dwell time threshold that an underboost condition must continuously persist before the controller increments the active adaptive wastegate cell in T1 control. When the throttle is initially opened, turbocharger spool lag naturally creates a temporary underboost condition. INCPT ensures that the error timer must accumulate a steady duration of underboost before the controller concludes that baseline duty cycle is truly insufficient, preventing transient spool-up lag from corrupting steady-state adaptive trims.
INCPT.overview_markdown: `INCPT` specifies the dwell time threshold that an underboost condition must continuously persist before the controller increments the active adaptive wastegate cell in T1 control. When the throttle is initially opened, turbocharger spool lag naturally creates a temporary underboost condition. `INCPT` ensures that the error timer must accumulate a steady duration of underboost before the controller concludes that baseline duty cycle is truly insufficient, preventing transient spool-up lag from corrupting steady-state adaptive trims.
INCPT.tuners_guide: Adjusting INCPT controls how quickly the adaptive system compensates for low boost. In factory calibrations, INCPT is set to 32 counts (approximately 0.35 seconds). Setting INCPT too low causes the controller to adapt upward prematurely during normal turbo lag, which can result in an overshoot once the turbo finally spools. Setting INCPT higher ensures that adaptive duty cycle additions occur only after prolonged, verified underboost, such as when driving in high gears or uphill under steady load.
INCPT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Underboost Dwell Time Threshold**: * Number of consecutive error timer counts that underboost must persist before the adaptive cell is incremented. * Factory setting is 32 counts (approximately 0.35 seconds).
* **Preventing Premature Adaptation on Lag**: * Higher values (40 to 60 counts, 0.45 to 0.7 seconds) prevent the ECU from adding duty cycle while a large turbo is naturally spooling.
* **Fast Convergence for Sluggish Spool**: * Lowering `INCPT` to 15 to 20 counts speeds up adaptive duty cycle additions if steady-state boost consistently falls short.
INCPT.operating_conditions:
Takes effect during part-throttle boost control, establishing the adaptive duty cycle increment time delay.

BRPMLO.overview: BRPMLO defines the lower engine speed boundary for in-flight atmospheric barometric pressure sampling during vehicle deceleration. Because turbocharged Chrysler engine controllers utilize a single manifold absolute pressure sensor to monitor both engine manifold pressure and ambient barometric pressure, the controller must periodically energize a baro read solenoid to vent the sensor to underhood atmosphere during closed-throttle deceleration. BRPMLO establishes the minimum engine speed required to permit this update. In factory calibrations, BRPMLO is configured to 1800 RPM. Below 1800 RPM, engine deceleration vacuum diminishes and the engine nears idle transition, which introduces pressure instability that would corrupt atmospheric measurements.
BRPMLO.overview_markdown: `BRPMLO` defines the lower engine speed boundary for in-flight atmospheric barometric pressure sampling during vehicle deceleration. Because turbocharged Chrysler engine controllers utilize a single manifold absolute pressure sensor to monitor both engine manifold pressure and ambient barometric pressure, the controller must periodically energize a baro read solenoid to vent the sensor to underhood atmosphere during closed-throttle deceleration. `BRPMLO` establishes the minimum engine speed required to permit this update. In factory calibrations, `BRPMLO` is configured to 1800 RPM. Below 1800 RPM, engine deceleration vacuum diminishes and the engine nears idle transition, which introduces pressure instability that would corrupt atmospheric measurements.
BRPMLO.tuners_guide: Raising BRPMLO narrows the permissible RPM window for deceleration baro updates, which can be useful when fitting aggressive high-overlap camshafts that produce erratic manifold pressure pulses at low to intermediate engine speeds. Lowering BRPMLO allows baro sampling deeper into a deceleration event, but setting BRPMLO below 1400 RPM risks allowing the controller to sample while the engine is falling toward base idle, potentially venting the sensor during an idle recovery flare. Most street and strip calibrations should retain BRPMLO near the factory 1800 RPM setting.
BRPMLO.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Aftermarket Camshaft Adjustments**: * If camshaft lope or weak low-RPM decel vacuum distorts baro readings, raise `BRPMLO` toward 2000 to 2200 RPM.
* **Idle Transition Buffer**: * Avoid setting `BRPMLO` below 1400 RPM to prevent venting the pressure sensor during dashpot idle capture.
* **Elevation Tracking Stability**: * Keeping `BRPMLO` near 1800 RPM ensures consistent in-flight elevation tracking during highway descents.

BRPMHI.overview: BRPMHI defines the upper engine speed boundary for in-flight atmospheric barometric pressure sampling during vehicle deceleration. When the driver lifts off the throttle from high engine speeds, intense exhaust scavenging, valvetrain harmonics, and rapid manifold pressure transients occur. Additionally, the driver is more likely to re-apply throttle abruptly during aggressive driving. BRPMHI prevents the controller from actuating the baro solenoid above this RPM ceiling. In factory calibrations, BRPMHI is configured to 6650 RPM (48000 counts in word format, representing approximately 6000 to 6650 RPM). If engine speed exceeds this ceiling, barometric reading requests are locked out until engine speed settles.

BRPMHI.tuners_guide: On modified engines that rev to 7000 RPM or higher, BRPMHI should be kept around 6000 to 6500 RPM to avoid switching the manifold pressure sensor to atmospheric vent while the engine is spinning at elevated rotational speeds. Venting the sensor at high engine speeds temporarily interrupts manifold pressure tracking; if the throttle snaps open while the sensor is vented, the controller may experience a momentary delay in delivering transient fuel enrichment. Lowering BRPMHI restricts baro updates to lower cruising speeds, which is safe for high-power drag race applications.
BRPMHI.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **High-RPM Safeguard**: * Keep `BRPMHI` below 6500 RPM to prevent venting the pressure sensor during aggressive high-RPM throttle lifts.
* **Transient Fueling Protection**: * Ensures the pressure sensor is never disconnected from manifold vacuum when rapid wide-open throttle reapplication is likely.
* **Drag Racing Recommendations**: * Leaving `BRPMHI` at factory settings prevents unwanted baro reads during high-RPM gear shifts.

BRDLAY.overview: BRDLAY defines the required duration of steady closed-throttle deceleration before the engine controller is permitted to initiate an in-flight barometric pressure reading. When the throttle plate abruptly closes from a cruising or boost condition, intake manifold pressure experiences severe pressure pulsations and pneumatic resonance before settling into stable closed-throttle vacuum. In factory calibrations, BRDLAY is configured to 182 counts, representing approximately 2.0 seconds. The throttle must remain continuously closed and engine speed must stay within the BRPMLO to BRPMHI window for 2.0 seconds before the barometric read solenoid is energized.

When the throttle plate abruptly closes from a cruising or boost condition, intake manifold pressure experiences severe pressure pulsations and pneumatic resonance before settling into stable closed-throttle vacuum. In factory calibrations, `BRDLAY` is configured to 182 counts, representing approximately 2.0 seconds. The throttle must remain continuously closed and engine speed must stay within the `BRPMLO` to `BRPMHI` window for 2.0 seconds before the barometric read solenoid is energized.
BRDLAY.tuners_guide: Lowering BRDLAY allows the controller to sample barometric pressure during shorter deceleration events, which can improve altitude tracking when driving through rapid mountain switchbacks with short downhill corners. However, setting BRDLAY below 1.0 second risks activating the baro solenoid while manifold air columns are still oscillating from throttle lift. Raising BRDLAY requires exceptionally long coastdown events before an in-flight baro reading can occur, which may prevent barometric updates from ever taking place in suburban driving.

* **Minimum Stabilization Limit**: * Keep `BRDLAY` at or above 1.0 second to ensure intake manifold pressure has fully settled.
* **Reset on Throttle Touch**: * Any touch of the accelerator immediately clears the countdown timer, resetting the stabilization period.

BARTIM.overview: BARTIM defines the minimum time interval required between successive in-flight barometric pressure updates. Atmospheric weather barometric pressure changes slowly over hours, and vehicular altitude changes occur over minutes. To prevent the barometric read solenoid from repeatedly cycling during frequent stop-and-go driving or repetitive throttle-lift cycles, BARTIM enforces a mandatory rest period between readings. In factory calibrations, BARTIM is set to 64 counts, representing approximately 179 seconds (approximately 3 minutes). Once an in-flight reading is taken, the controller locks out further baro reads until this 3-minute timer elapses.

Atmospheric weather barometric pressure changes slowly over hours, and vehicular altitude changes occur over minutes. To prevent the barometric read solenoid from repeatedly cycling during frequent stop-and-go driving or repetitive throttle-lift cycles, `BARTIM` enforces a mandatory rest period between readings. In factory calibrations, `BARTIM` is set to 64 counts, representing approximately 179 seconds (approximately 3 minutes). Once an in-flight reading is taken, the controller locks out further baro reads until this 3-minute timer elapses.
BARTIM.tuners_guide: Lowering BARTIM allows more frequent barometric pressure sampling, which is advantageous for hill-climb competition or mountain driving where road elevation changes by thousands of feet within a short drive. Reducing BARTIM to 60 or 90 seconds improves altitude fuel trimming responsiveness. However, lowering BARTIM below 30 seconds causes excessive solenoid cycling. Raising BARTIM extends the lock-out interval, keeping the existing baro value locked in memory longer. Setting BARTIM to maximum (255 counts) suppresses in-flight updates, relying almost entirely on the key-on barometric reading.
BARTIM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Mountain Hill-Climb Racing**: * Lower `BARTIM` to 60 to 90 seconds to adapt fueling quickly to rapid altitude ascents.
* **Preventing Excessive Solenoid Wear**: * Do not set `BARTIM` below 30 seconds to avoid relentless cycling of the pneumatic solenoid.
* **Key-On Reliance**: * Setting `BARTIM` to 255 counts effectively locks barometric pressure to the initial engine startup reading.

BROPTM.overview: BROPTM defines the pneumatic stabilization delay after the barometric read solenoid is energized before the engine controller reads the manifold absolute pressure sensor voltage. When the baro solenoid is energized, it closes the port connecting the sensor to intake manifold vacuum and opens a vent to underhood atmospheric air. Because air must physically flow through the vacuum harness to fill the vacuum line and sensor cavity up to atmospheric pressure, an instantaneous reading would measure residual vacuum, falsely recording lower barometric pressure. In factory calibrations, BROPTM is set to 9 counts, providing approximately 0.10 seconds (100 milliseconds) of pressure equalization time before sampling.
BROPTM.overview_markdown: `BROPTM` defines the pneumatic stabilization delay after the barometric read solenoid is energized before the engine controller reads the manifold absolute pressure sensor voltage. When the baro solenoid is energized, it closes the port connecting the sensor to intake manifold vacuum and opens a vent to underhood atmospheric air. Because air must physically flow through the vacuum harness to fill the vacuum line and sensor cavity up to atmospheric pressure, an instantaneous reading would measure residual vacuum, falsely recording lower barometric pressure. In factory calibrations, `BROPTM` is set to 9 counts, providing approximately 0.10 seconds (100 milliseconds) of pressure equalization time before sampling.
BROPTM.tuners_guide: If aftermarket vacuum lines to the pressure sensor have been lengthened, or if an inline pneumatic pulsation dampener or filter is installed in the sensor line, pneumatic pressure equalization requires more time. In such custom setups, increasing BROPTM to 150 or 200 milliseconds (14 to 19 counts) ensures complete atmospheric venting and prevents skewed altitude calculations. Lowering BROPTM below 80 milliseconds risks sampling while vacuum is still dissipating, causing the controller to record an artificially low barometric reading that leads to lean high-altitude fuel trimming.
BROPTM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Long Vacuum Hose Routing**: * Raise `BROPTM` to 14 to 18 counts (150 to 200 ms) if relocated pressure sensors use extended vacuum lines.
* **Pneumatic Dampener Installations**: * Inline orifice restrictors or filters slow venting; increase `BROPTM` to allow complete atmospheric equalization.
* **Under-Reporting Prevention**: * Never set `BROPTM` below 6 counts (~60 ms) to avoid sampling lingering manifold vacuum.

BROPTM.raw_text: BROPTM defines the pneumatic stabilization delay after the barometric read solenoid is energized before the engine controller reads the manifold absolute pressure sensor voltage. If aftermarket vacuum lines to the pressure sensor have been lengthened, or if an inline pneumatic pulsation dampener or filter is installed in the sensor line, pneumatic pressure equalization requires more time.

BRCLTM.overview: BRCLTM defines the pneumatic stabilization delay after the barometric read solenoid is de-energized before the engine controller resumes using sensor readings for manifold pressure calculations. After the atmospheric barometric reading has been captured, the controller de-energizes the solenoid, closing the atmospheric vent and reconnecting the sensor to the intake manifold. Because the sensor cavity and vacuum line are filled with atmospheric air, manifold vacuum must draw this air out to restore true engine vacuum. In factory calibrations, BRCLTM is configured to 9 counts, providing approximately 0.10 seconds (100 milliseconds) for line vacuum re-establishment before the controller trusts MAP sensor data.
BRCLTM.overview_markdown: `BRCLTM` defines the pneumatic stabilization delay after the barometric read solenoid is de-energized before the engine controller resumes using sensor readings for manifold pressure calculations. After the atmospheric barometric reading has been captured, the controller de-energizes the solenoid, closing the atmospheric vent and reconnecting the sensor to the intake manifold. Because the sensor cavity and vacuum line are filled with atmospheric air, manifold vacuum must draw this air out to restore true engine vacuum. In factory calibrations, `BRCLTM` is configured to 9 counts, providing approximately 0.10 seconds (100 milliseconds) for line vacuum re-establishment before the controller trusts MAP sensor data.
BRCLTM.tuners_guide: Maintaining proper delay in BRCLTM prevents false transient enrichments upon throttle reapplication. If BRCLTM is set too low (below 50 milliseconds), the controller may sample lingering atmospheric pressure while the vacuum line is still evacuating, mistaking the higher pressure for sudden throttle opening and commanding unnecessary acceleration enrichment. For engines with lengthy pressure sensor vacuum hoses, increasing BRCLTM to 150 milliseconds (14 counts) guarantees that true intake manifold vacuum is fully re-established before fuel and spark tables read the sensor.
BRCLTM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Preventing False Tip-In Enrichment**: * If `BRCLTM` is too short, residual atmospheric air looks like manifold boost, triggering false acceleration enrichment.
* **Hose Volume Compensation**: * Increase `BRCLTM` to 12 to 15 counts (130 to 160 ms) if relocated sensors use long vacuum plumbing.
* **Quick Throttle Recovery**: * Retaining ~100 ms ensures rapid return to closed-loop fuel and spark tracking.

BAROHI.overview: BAROHI defines the maximum credible atmospheric pressure threshold used during barometric pressure validation. When the engine controller samples barometric pressure at key-on or during closed-throttle deceleration, it evaluates the measured reading against BAROHI to verify sensor plausibility. Standard sea level atmospheric pressure is approximately 14.7 psi absolute (29.9 inHg), and extreme meteorological high-pressure weather cells rarely exceed 15.2 psi absolute. In factory calibrations, BAROHI is configured to 133 counts, corresponding to approximately 15.3 psi absolute (31.1 inHg). If an atmospheric reading equals or exceeds BAROHI, the controller identifies the measurement as electrically implausible (such as a 5-volt reference short or broken sensor ground) and substitutes the failsafe default value BARDFT.

When the engine controller samples barometric pressure at key-on or during closed-throttle deceleration, it evaluates the measured reading against `BAROHI` to verify sensor plausibility. Standard sea level atmospheric pressure is approximately 14.7 psi absolute (29.9 inHg), and extreme meteorological high-pressure weather cells rarely exceed 15.2 psi absolute. In factory calibrations, `BAROHI` is configured to 133 counts, corresponding to approximately 15.3 psi absolute (31.1 inHg). If an atmospheric reading equals or exceeds `BAROHI`, the controller identifies the measurement as electrically implausible (such as a 5-volt reference short or broken sensor ground) and substitutes the failsafe default value `BARDFT`.
BAROHI.tuners_guide: When converting to a 3-bar MAP sensor, BAROHI must be rescaled. On a factory 2-bar sensor, 0 to 5 volts spans 0 to 29.4 psi absolute, placing sea level atmospheric pressure near 128 counts. On a 3-bar sensor, 0 to 5 volts spans 0 to 44.1 psi absolute, which places sea level atmospheric pressure at approximately 85 counts, and a 15.3 psi upper plausibility limit at approximately 88 counts. If BAROHI is left uncalibrated at 133 counts on a 3-bar setup, an implausible or shorted sensor reading up to 23 psi absolute could be accepted as valid atmospheric pressure, severely corrupting altitude fuel corrections and overboost cutout limits.
BAROHI.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **3-Bar MAP Sensor Rescaling**: * On a 3-bar sensor, rescale `BAROHI` from factory 133 counts down to ~88 counts (15.2 psi on 44.1 psi scale).
* **Failsafe Substitution**: * Any reading meeting or exceeding `BAROHI` is immediately rejected, and `BARDFT` is loaded into memory.
* **Diagnostic Protection**: * Protects fuel calibration against high-voltage sensor wire shorts and disconnected sensor ground circuits.
BAROHI.operating_conditions:
Takes effect during key-on and in-flight barometric pressure reads, establishing the acceptable high voltage limit for a valid atmospheric reading.

BAROLO.overview: BAROLO defines the minimum credible atmospheric pressure threshold used during barometric pressure validation. When the engine controller reads ambient barometric pressure, it verifies that the measurement is above BAROLO before storing it into RAM. Atmospheric pressure at 14,000 feet elevation (such as Pikes Peak highway) is approximately 8.6 psi absolute (17.5 inHg). In factory calibrations, BAROLO is set to 69 counts, representing approximately 7.9 psi absolute (16.1 inHg). Any ambient reading below BAROLO indicates a defective sensor, pinched vacuum line, or a baro read solenoid that failed to open to atmosphere. If a reading falls below BAROLO, it is rejected and BARDFT is loaded instead.
BAROLO.overview_markdown: `BAROLO` defines the minimum credible atmospheric pressure threshold used during barometric pressure validation. When the engine controller reads ambient barometric pressure, it verifies that the measurement is above `BAROLO` before storing it into RAM. Atmospheric pressure at 14,000 feet elevation (such as Pikes Peak highway) is approximately 8.6 psi absolute (17.5 inHg). In factory calibrations, `BAROLO` is set to 69 counts, representing approximately 7.9 psi absolute (16.1 inHg). Any ambient reading below `BAROLO` indicates a defective sensor, pinched vacuum line, or a baro read solenoid that failed to open to atmosphere. If a reading falls below `BAROLO`, it is rejected and `BARDFT` is loaded instead.
BAROLO.tuners_guide: When converting to a 3-bar MAP sensor, BAROLO must be rescaled downward. On a 3-bar sensor, 7.9 psi absolute corresponds to approximately 46 counts on the 0 to 44.1 psi scale. If BAROLO is left at the stock 69 counts on a 3-bar sensor, normal driving at high altitudes (above 6,000 feet, where atmospheric pressure drops below 11.8 psi / 68 counts) will falsely trigger the low plausibility limit, locking barometric pressure to BARDFT and disabling proper altitude fueling corrections. Lowering BAROLO to ~44 counts preserves valid altitude tracking up to 14,000 feet on 3-bar setups.
BAROLO.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **3-Bar MAP High-Altitude Operation**: * Rescale `BAROLO` to ~44 to 46 counts on 3-bar sensors to prevent false fault substitution when driving above 6,000 feet.
* **Fault Detection Integrity**: * Setting `BAROLO` too low allows a stuck-shut baro solenoid to feed engine vacuum into `BaroPressure` undetected.
* **Default Substitution**: * Rejection of a reading below `BAROLO` forces immediate fallback to `BARDFT`.

BARDFT.overview: BARDFT defines the failsafe default atmospheric barometric pressure value loaded into memory whenever a measured barometric reading fails sensor plausibility verification. If an atmospheric reading falls below BAROLO or exceeds BAROHI, the engine controller identifies the measurement as untrustworthy and immediately substitutes BARDFT. In factory calibrations, BARDFT is set to 127 counts, corresponding to approximately 14.6 psi absolute (29.7 inHg), representing standard nominal sea level atmospheric pressure. This ensures that in the event of a pressure sensor disconnect, pinched hose, or solenoid failure, the engine continues running safely with predictable sea level fuel and spark parameters.
BARDFT.overview_markdown: `BARDFT` defines the failsafe default atmospheric barometric pressure value loaded into memory whenever a measured barometric reading fails sensor plausibility verification. If an atmospheric reading falls below `BAROLO` or exceeds `BAROHI`, the engine controller identifies the measurement as untrustworthy and immediately substitutes `BARDFT`. In factory calibrations, `BARDFT` is set to 127 counts, corresponding to approximately 14.6 psi absolute (29.7 inHg), representing standard nominal sea level atmospheric pressure. This ensures that in the event of a pressure sensor disconnect, pinched hose, or solenoid failure, the engine continues running safely with predictable sea level fuel and spark parameters.
BARDFT.tuners_guide: BARDFT must be rescaled whenever upgrading to a 3-bar MAP sensor. On a factory 2-bar sensor, 14.6 psi absolute corresponds to 127 counts on the 0 to 29.4 psi span. On a 3-bar sensor, 14.6 psi absolute corresponds to approximately 85 counts on the 0 to 44.1 psi span. Leaving BARDFT at 127 counts on a 3-bar setup would cause the controller, upon any sensor fault, to substitute an apparent barometric pressure of 22 psi absolute. This would induce extreme fuel over-enrichment and severely distort boost cutout calculations. Always rescale BARDFT to ~85 counts for 3-bar conversions.
BARDFT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Mandatory 3-Bar Rescaling**: * Set `BARDFT` to ~85 counts on 3-bar MAP conversions to represent standard 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure.
* **Failsafe Fueling Anchor**: * Acts as the emergency anchor for fuel, spark, and overboost protection if sensor wiring is damaged.
* **Elevation Bias Tuning**: * For vehicles operated exclusively at high elevation (e.g. Denver at 5,000 feet), `BARDFT` can be adjusted to 12.2 psi.
BARDFT.operating_conditions:
Takes effect as a failsafe default whenever barometric pressure cannot be read or a MAP sensor fault occurs, defaulting atmospheric pressure to sea level (29.92 inHg) to keep fueling safe.

FANTMP1.overview: FANTMP1 defines the engine coolant temperature threshold required to energize the radiator cooling fan when the vehicle is traveling at highway speeds above 45 MPH. At higher road speeds, natural forward ram airflow through the front fascia and radiator core provides substantial convective heat rejection without needing the electric cooling fan. To conserve electrical power and prolong fan motor life, the engine controller raises the temperature threshold required to start the fan when cruising at highway speeds. In factory calibrations, FANTMP1 is set to 232 counts, corresponding to approximately 204 °F. If engine coolant temperature exceeds this point at highway speed, the controller energizes the fan relay to assist cooling under heavy sustained cruise loads.
FANTMP1.overview_markdown: `FANTMP1` defines the engine coolant temperature threshold required to energize the radiator cooling fan when the vehicle is traveling at highway speeds above 45 MPH. At higher road speeds, natural forward ram airflow through the front fascia and radiator core provides substantial convective heat rejection without needing the electric cooling fan. To conserve electrical power and prolong fan motor life, the engine controller raises the temperature threshold required to start the fan when cruising at highway speeds. In factory calibrations, `FANTMP1` is set to 232 counts, corresponding to approximately 204 °F. If engine coolant temperature exceeds this point at highway speed, the controller energizes the fan relay to assist cooling under heavy sustained cruise loads.
FANTMP1.tuners_guide: Lowering FANTMP1 turns the cooling fan on at cooler operating temperatures during highway cruising, which is essential when installing a 160 °F or 180 °F performance thermostat. For a 180 °F thermostat, lowering FANTMP1 to approximately 192 °F to 196 °F maintains cooler combustion chambers and lowers intake charge temperatures under sustained boost. Raising FANTMP1 delays fan activation, relying entirely on vehicle speed airflow. Always keep FANTMP1 at least 4 to 6 °F higher than its companion turn-off parameter FANTMP2 to preserve hysteresis and prevent relay chattering.
FANTMP1.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Thermostat Matching**: * For 180 °F thermostats, lower `FANTMP1` from factory 204 °F down to 192 °F to 196 °F. * For 160 °F thermostats, lower `FANTMP1` down to 176 °F to 180 °F.
* **Hysteresis Relationship**: * Maintain a 4 to 6 °F spread above `FANTMP2` to prevent rapid cycling of the fan relay at cruising speeds.
FANTMP1.operating_conditions:
Takes effect when engine coolant temperature rises to this threshold (or at highway cruising speeds above 45 MPH), commanding the electric radiator cooling fan ON.

FANTMP2.overview: FANTMP2 defines the engine coolant temperature threshold where the radiator cooling fan is turned off after a highway cooling cycle above 45 MPH. Once the cooling fan is engaged at high vehicle speed, it continues running until coolant temperature is driven down below FANTMP2. In factory calibrations, FANTMP2 is set to 227 counts, corresponding to approximately 199 °F. This establishes a 5 °F hysteresis buffer below the turn-on setpoint (204 °F), preventing rapid cycling and relay flutter while driving on the highway.
FANTMP2.overview_markdown: `FANTMP2` defines the engine coolant temperature threshold where the radiator cooling fan is turned off after a highway cooling cycle above 45 MPH. Once the cooling fan is engaged at high vehicle speed, it continues running until coolant temperature is driven down below `FANTMP2`. In factory calibrations, `FANTMP2` is set to 227 counts, corresponding to approximately 199 °F. This establishes a 5 °F hysteresis buffer below the turn-on setpoint (204 °F), preventing rapid cycling and relay flutter while driving on the highway.
FANTMP2.tuners_guide: When lowering FANTMP1 for a cooler thermostat, FANTMP2 must be lowered proportionally to maintain an adequate hysteresis deadband. For a 180 °F thermostat setup with FANTMP1 at 194 °F, set FANTMP2 to approximately 188 °F. Never calibrate FANTMP2 below the thermostat mechanical opening temperature, as the engine cannot cool below that point, causing the fan to run continuously. Setting FANTMP2 too close to FANTMP1 causes frequent on-off cycling on slight engine load changes.
FANTMP2.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Proportional Downward Shift**: * Lower `FANTMP2` alongside `FANTMP1` when fitting a cooler thermostat (e.g. 188 °F for a 180 °F thermostat).
* **Thermostat Rating Floor**: * Ensure `FANTMP2` is at least 4 to 6 °F above the thermostat mechanical rating so the fan can shut off.
* **Deadband Width**: * Retain a 4 to 6 °F gap below `FANTMP1` to avoid relay chatter.

FANTMP3.overview: FANTMP3 defines the coolant temperature threshold that energizes the radiator cooling fan during low-speed driving or idle conditions below 35 MPH. When stopped in traffic or driving at low vehicle speeds, no ram airflow enters the front grille to cool the radiator and intercooler cores. Underhood temperatures quickly rise from the turbocharger turbine housing and exhaust manifold. In factory calibrations, FANTMP3 is set to 227 counts, corresponding to approximately 199 °F. When coolant temperature exceeds this threshold, the controller turns on the electric cooling fan to draw airflow through the cooling pack, preventing engine overheating during city operation.

When stopped in traffic or driving at low vehicle speeds, no ram airflow enters the front grille to cool the radiator and intercooler cores. Underhood temperatures quickly rise from the turbocharger turbine housing and exhaust manifold. In factory calibrations, `FANTMP3` is set to 227 counts, corresponding to approximately 199 °F. When coolant temperature exceeds this threshold, the controller turns on the electric cooling fan to draw airflow through the cooling pack, preventing engine overheating during city operation.
FANTMP3.tuners_guide: FANTMP3 is the primary parameter tuners modify to control engine operating temperature in stop-and-go driving. When converting to a 180 °F thermostat, lowering FANTMP3 to 188 °F to 192 °F keeps cylinder head and intake charge temperatures lower, significantly reducing heat soak and tip-in spark knock away from stoplights. When using a 160 °F thermostat, lower FANTMP3 to approximately 172 °F to 176 °F. Always maintain FANTMP3 higher than the shutoff threshold FANTMP4 by at least 5 °F to prevent erratic relay toggling.
FANTMP3.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Primary Fan Tuning Target**: * Most frequently adjusted cooling parameter; controls stationary idle and slow-traffic engine temperature.
* **Thermostat Calibration**: * 180 °F thermostat: calibrate `FANTMP3` between 188 °F and 192 °F. * 160 °F thermostat: calibrate `FANTMP3` between 172 °F and 176 °F.
* **Detonation Resistance**: * Keeping city idle coolant temperatures below 195 °F sharply reduces manifold heat soak and launch knock.
FANTMP3.operating_conditions:
Takes effect when driving in slow city traffic or idling below 35 MPH, commanding the radiator cooling fan ON once coolant temperature reaches this threshold.

FANTMP4.overview: FANTMP4 defines the engine coolant temperature threshold where the cooling fan shuts off after completing a low-speed cooling cycle below 35 MPH. After the fan engages at low speed or idle (triggered by FANTMP3), it remains energized until coolant temperature is reduced below FANTMP4. This creates an approximate 5 to 6 °F hysteresis cushion below the 199 °F turn-on threshold, ensuring the fan runs long enough to achieve meaningful cooling before shutting down.

FANMAP.overview: FANMAP defines the turbocharger boost pressure threshold relative to barometric pressure that turns on the radiator and intercooler cooling fan. In factory turbocharged vehicles where the radiator and intercooler share the forward front-end airflow duct, sustained turbo boost generates localized charge air heating and underhood thermal stress. When manifold pressure exceeds barometric pressure by FANMAP, the engine controller energizes the cooling fan regardless of coolant temperature, drawing extra airflow through the intercooler core. In factory 2.5L ATX calibrations, FANMAP is configured to 255 counts (29.4 psi boost), effectively disabling this boost-activated fan feature for conservative commuter driving.

When manifold pressure exceeds barometric pressure by `FANMAP`, the engine controller energizes the cooling fan regardless of coolant temperature, drawing extra airflow through the intercooler core. In factory 2.5L ATX calibrations, `FANMAP` is configured to 255 counts (29.4 psi boost), effectively disabling this boost-activated fan feature for conservative commuter driving.
FANMAP.tuners_guide: For performance and intercooled calibrations, lowering FANMAP to approximately 2.0 to 4.0 psi of boost (17 to 35 counts) energizes the cooling fan during boost spool-up. This pulls fresh ambient air across the intercooler and radiator during hard acceleration, reducing intake charge heat soak and lowering cylinder head temperatures on road-course or drag strip passes. Setting FANMAP too low (under 1.0 psi) causes unnecessary fan cycling during light-throttle highway cruising. When converting to a 3-bar MAP sensor, FANMAP must be rescaled to match the expanded 44.1 psi pressure range. Setting FANMAP to 255 counts disables boost-activated cooling.

* **Intercooler Heat Soak Prevention**: * Lower `FANMAP` to 2.0 to 4.0 psi boost (17 to 35 counts) to spool the fan upon turbo boost onset.
* **3-Bar MAP Scaling**: * Rescale `FANMAP` for 3-bar conversions to account for the wider 0 to 44.1 psi absolute sensor calibration.
* **Disabling Boost-Triggered Fan**: * Set `FANMAP` to 255 counts (factory setting) to prevent boost from activating the radiator fan.
FANMAP.operating_conditions:
Takes effect under positive turbo boost pressure, turning the cooling fan ON when manifold pressure exceeds barometric pressure by this amount to lower charge temperatures.

FANBAT.overview: FANBAT defines the underhood temperature threshold measured at the battery tray thermistor that triggers radiator cooling fan activation. In turbocharged Chrysler vehicles, high underhood radiant heat from the turbocharger turbine housing and exhaust manifold can accumulate in the engine compartment during low-speed driving or after hard boost runs. Because the battery and the engine controller power module share the engine compartment behind the left headlight, extreme heat degrades lead-acid battery life and reduces alternator voltage regulation efficiency. In factory calibrations, FANBAT is set to 27 counts, corresponding to approximately 120 °F. If battery temperature rises above this threshold, the controller energizes the cooling fan to evacuate hot air from the engine bay.

In turbocharged Chrysler vehicles, high underhood radiant heat from the turbocharger turbine housing and exhaust manifold can accumulate in the engine compartment during low-speed driving or after hard boost runs. Because the battery and the engine controller power module share the engine compartment behind the left headlight, extreme heat degrades lead-acid battery life and reduces alternator voltage regulation efficiency. In factory calibrations, `FANBAT` is set to 27 counts, corresponding to approximately 120 °F. If battery temperature rises above this threshold, the controller energizes the cooling fan to evacuate hot air from the engine bay.
FANBAT.tuners_guide: Lowering FANBAT causes the cooling fan to engage at cooler underhood temperatures, which is beneficial for tight engine compartments (such as Dodge Omni or Charger GLH bodies) where turbo heat buildup is intense. Raising FANBAT delays underhood heat-triggered fan activation. If the battery tray temperature sensor is disconnected, defective, or deleted during a battery trunk relocation, the sensor circuit defaults toward high resistance (low counts / apparent high temperature), which can cause the radiator fan to run continuously. In battery-relocated vehicles, ensure the sensor is properly terminated or set FANBAT high to prevent unwanted fan activation.
FANBAT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Tight Engine Bay Heat Management**: * Lower `FANBAT` to 110 °F to 115 °F on cramped L-body and G-body turbo cars to purge radiant exhaust heat.
* **Battery Relocation Safeguard**: * If the battery is relocated to the trunk and the thermistor is deleted, set `FANBAT` high to prevent false fan triggers.
* **Sensor Inversion Note**: * The battery thermistor uses negative temperature coefficient logic; lower sensor voltage counts represent higher physical temperature.
FANBAT.operating_conditions:
Takes effect when underhood battery tray temperature rises above this threshold, turning the radiator cooling fan ON to flush stagnant hot air from the engine bay.

FNSPHI.overview: FNSPHI defines the high vehicle speed transition threshold that switches the cooling fan logic between low-speed city mode and high-speed highway mode. The engine controller monitors road speed via the transmission distance sensor, which stores the pulse period between speedometer pulses in high-byte variable VehicleSpeed_HB. Because this variable measures time duration between pulses, smaller count values represent faster road speeds. In factory calibrations, FNSPHI is set to 11 counts, representing approximately 44 MPH. When road speed exceeds this threshold, the controller switches from low-speed fan setpoints (FANTMP3/FANTMP4) to highway setpoints (FANTMP1/FANTMP2).

Because this variable measures time duration between pulses, smaller count values represent faster road speeds. When road speed exceeds this threshold, the controller switches from low-speed fan setpoints (`FANTMP3`/`FANTMP4`) to highway setpoints (`FANTMP1`/`FANTMP2`).

Lowering FNSPHI in counts raises the speed in miles per hour required to enter highway mode, keeping the more aggressive low-speed fan thresholds active up to higher cruising speeds. Raising FNSPHI in counts causes highway mode to engage at lower vehicle speeds. Tuners typically leave FNSPHI at factory settings unless altering final drive gear ratios or tire diameters, which shifts speedometer pulse frequency.

* **Pulse Period Inversion**: * Lower count values in `FNSPHI` represent higher road speeds in miles per hour.
* **Speed Hysteresis Window**: * Works with `FNSPLO` to prevent fan threshold hunting when driving at moderate speeds (36 to 44 MPH).
* **Tire & Gear Ratio Changes**: * Adjust `FNSPHI` if significant tire diameter or final drive gear changes alter speedometer pulse calibration.

PURMAP.overview: PURMAP establishes the intake manifold vacuum margin required below atmospheric barometric pressure to enable the evaporative emission canister purge solenoid. The evaporative emission system draws stored fuel vapors from the charcoal canister into the engine intake manifold using engine vacuum. On turbocharged engines, under boost or wide-open throttle, intake manifold pressure becomes positive relative to atmospheric pressure. If the canister purge solenoid opened during boost, pressurized intake air would blow backwards through the purge lines into the charcoal canister and fuel tank. In factory calibrations, PURMAP is set to 5 counts, corresponding to approximately 0.6 psi (1.2 inHg) of vacuum below barometric pressure. Manifold pressure must stay at least this far below atmospheric pressure before purge is permitted.

The evaporative emission system draws stored fuel vapors from the charcoal canister into the engine intake manifold using engine vacuum. On turbocharged engines, under boost or wide-open throttle, intake manifold pressure becomes positive relative to atmospheric pressure. If the canister purge solenoid opened during boost, pressurized intake air would blow backwards through the purge lines into the charcoal canister and fuel tank. In factory calibrations, `PURMAP` is set to 5 counts, corresponding to approximately 0.6 psi (1.2 inHg) of vacuum below barometric pressure. Manifold pressure must stay at least this far below atmospheric pressure before purge is permitted.
PURMAP.tuners_guide: When converting to a 3-bar MAP sensor, PURMAP should be checked and rescaled. On a 3-bar sensor, 5 counts represents a wider pressure delta (~0.86 psi), requiring deeper engine vacuum before canister purge opens. Raising PURMAP requires deeper intake manifold vacuum before purge engages, restricting purge operation to light deceleration or high-vacuum cruising. Lowering PURMAP allows purge closer to atmospheric zero, but setting it too close to zero risks back-pressuring the evaporative canister during rapid throttle snap-open transients before the solenoid can close. In Turbonator calibrations configured for an RPM shift light, the purge solenoid output circuit is often repurposed to drive the shift light indicator.
PURMAP.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **3-Bar MAP Scaling**: * Verify and rescale `PURMAP` on 3-bar sensor conversions to maintain proper vacuum margins on the 44.1 psi scale.
* **Boost Backflow Protection**: * Software failsafe that guarantees the purge valve closes before intake pressure reaches atmospheric zero or positive boost.
* **Shift Light Repurposing**: * When option bit `cfg_PurgeShiftLight` is enabled in Turbonator calibrations, this output drives the driver shift light.

PURHYS.overview: PURHYS defines the vacuum hysteresis deadband for the evaporative canister purge solenoid control routine. When driving at steady cruising speeds near light throttle, intake manifold vacuum naturally oscillates due to road irregularities and small throttle pedal movements. If the controller used a single fixed vacuum threshold to toggle the purge solenoid, the valve would buzz or chatter rapidly on and off. In factory calibrations, PURHYS is configured to 2 counts, providing approximately 0.23 psi (0.5 inHg) of hysteresis. Once canister purge is energized, PURHYS is subtracted from the barometric headroom, requiring manifold pressure to rise closer to atmospheric pressure before the solenoid is shut off.

When driving at steady cruising speeds near light throttle, intake manifold vacuum naturally oscillates due to road irregularities and small throttle pedal movements. If the controller used a single fixed vacuum threshold to toggle the purge solenoid, the valve would buzz or chatter rapidly on and off. In factory calibrations, `PURHYS` is configured to 2 counts, providing approximately 0.23 psi (0.5 inHg) of hysteresis. Once canister purge is energized, `PURHYS` is subtracted from the barometric headroom, requiring manifold pressure to rise closer to atmospheric pressure before the solenoid is shut off.
PURHYS.tuners_guide: Retain the factory setting of 2 counts for normal street operation. Increasing PURHYS widens the hysteresis deadband, preventing purge shutdown during minor throttle tip-ins and keeping the valve flowing vapors steadily under variable cruise loads. Setting PURHYS too high keeps the purge solenoid energized dangerously close to atmospheric pressure where manifold boost onset is imminent. Lowering PURHYS to zero removes all hysteresis, which causes audible clicking and mechanical wear of the solenoid when driving at light highway throttle.
PURHYS.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Hysteresis Deadband Preservation**: * Keep `PURHYS` at factory 2 counts (~0.5 inHg) for quiet, stable purge valve operation.
* **Preventing Solenoid Chatter**: * Zeroing `PURHYS` produces rapid on-off clicking on rough pavement or highway undulations.
* **Upper Limit Caution**: * Do not raise `PURHYS` beyond 4 counts to avoid delaying purge shutoff as the engine transitions into boost.

PURTMP.overview: PURTMP defines the minimum engine coolant temperature required to enable evaporative canister purge operation. When an engine is warming up from a cold start, fuel atomization is inefficient, combustion chamber walls are cold, and the engine operates in open-loop fuel enrichment. Introducing unmetered raw hydrocarbon vapors from the carbon canister into a cold intake manifold destabilizes warmup fueling, causing rough idle, spark plug fouling, or engine stalling. In factory calibrations, PURTMP is configured to 130 counts, corresponding to approximately 130 °F. Until engine coolant reaches this temperature, the controller holds the canister purge solenoid closed.
PURTMP.overview_markdown: `PURTMP` defines the minimum engine coolant temperature required to enable evaporative canister purge operation. When an engine is warming up from a cold start, fuel atomization is inefficient, combustion chamber walls are cold, and the engine operates in open-loop fuel enrichment. Introducing unmetered raw hydrocarbon vapors from the carbon canister into a cold intake manifold destabilizes warmup fueling, causing rough idle, spark plug fouling, or engine stalling. In factory calibrations, `PURTMP` is configured to 130 counts, corresponding to approximately 130 °F. Until engine coolant reaches this temperature, the controller holds the canister purge solenoid closed.
PURTMP.tuners_guide: Raising PURTMP to 160 °F or 170 °F delays canister purge until the engine has completely warmed up and settled into fully adapted closed-loop oxygen sensor control. This is advantageous for modified engines equipped with aggressive camshaft profiles, large performance fuel injectors, or ethanol fuel blends where idle stability during warmup is fragile. Lowering PURTMP allows purge to begin earlier, but setting PURTMP below 120 °F risks introducing vapor surges while the engine is still warming up, causing hunting idle and hesitation during light throttle driving.
PURTMP.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Warmup Idle Stabilization**: * Raise `PURTMP` to 160 °F to 170 °F on big-cam or large-injector setups to prevent vapor-induced idle hunting during warmup.
* **Cold Start Protection**: * Do not lower `PURTMP` below 120 °F to avoid rich stumbling before closed-loop oxygen sensor feedback is active.
* **Emissions Compliance**: * Factory 130 °F setting achieves early canister purge without compromising cold drivability.

ACLRPM.overview: ACLRPM defines the low engine speed emergency anti-stall cutout threshold for the air conditioning compressor clutch. An automotive air conditioning compressor imposes several horsepower of mechanical parasitic drag on the engine crankshaft. If engine speed suddenly plummets due to abrupt clutch release, panic braking with locked wheels, or idle air instability, dragging the mechanical compressor will cause the engine to stall. In factory calibrations, ACLRPM is set to 4000 counts (corresponding to 500 RPM in 16-bit word format). When engine speed drops below this safety floor, the controller immediately de-energizes the A/C clutch relay, dumping compressor load so the engine can catch and revive.
ACLRPM.overview_markdown: `ACLRPM` defines the low engine speed emergency anti-stall cutout threshold for the air conditioning compressor clutch. An automotive air conditioning compressor imposes several horsepower of mechanical parasitic drag on the engine crankshaft. If engine speed suddenly plummets due to abrupt clutch release, panic braking with locked wheels, or idle air instability, dragging the mechanical compressor will cause the engine to stall. In factory calibrations, `ACLRPM` is set to 4000 counts (corresponding to 500 RPM in 16-bit word format). When engine speed drops below this safety floor, the controller immediately de-energizes the A/C clutch relay, dumping compressor load so the engine can catch and revive.
ACLRPM.tuners_guide: Raising ACLRPM to 600 or 700 RPM provides an earlier anti-stall safety net, which is highly recommended for lightweight flywheel installations, aggressive camshafts with low idle vacuum, or manual transmission conversions where sudden RPM dips occur when coming to a quick stop. Setting ACLRPM too close to target idle speed (e.g. within 50 RPM) can cause the compressor to short-cycle and disengage momentarily whenever idle dips slightly in gear. Never lower ACLRPM below 450 RPM, as doing so negates stall protection.
ACLRPM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Lightweight Flywheel Anti-Stall**: * Raise `ACLRPM` to 600 to 700 RPM to dump compressor drag sooner during rapid deceleration dips.
* **Performance Camshaft Lope**: * Ensure `ACLRPM` sits comfortably below the lowest trough of idle lope to prevent unwanted A/C disengagement.
* **Lower Limit Rule**: * Keep at or above 450 RPM to protect against stalling during panic stops.
ACLRPM.operating_conditions:
Takes effect whenever engine RPM drops dangerously low near stall speed while the air conditioning is operating, cutting compressor clutch drag so the engine can catch and revive.

ACOUT.overview: ACOUT defines the throttle position sensor voltage delta above learned closed throttle (MINTHR) that disengages the air conditioning compressor clutch during heavy acceleration. When the driver depresses the accelerator pedal for passing, merging, or wide-open throttle acceleration, disengaging the mechanical A/C compressor eliminates 5 to 10 horsepower of parasitic crankshaft load, delivering maximum engine power to the drive wheels. In factory calibrations, ACOUT is configured to 133 counts, corresponding to approximately 2.60 Volts above closed throttle (approximately 70% to 75% throttle opening). Once throttle opening exceeds this threshold, the controller cuts off the A/C clutch, smoothly re-engaging it when the throttle is released.
ACOUT.overview_markdown: `ACOUT` defines the throttle position sensor voltage delta above learned closed throttle (`MINTHR`) that disengages the air conditioning compressor clutch during heavy acceleration. When the driver depresses the accelerator pedal for passing, merging, or wide-open throttle acceleration, disengaging the mechanical A/C compressor eliminates 5 to 10 horsepower of parasitic crankshaft load, delivering maximum engine power to the drive wheels. In factory calibrations, `ACOUT` is configured to 133 counts, corresponding to approximately 2.60 Volts above closed throttle (approximately 70% to 75% throttle opening). Once throttle opening exceeds this threshold, the controller cuts off the A/C clutch, smoothly re-engaging it when the throttle is released.
ACOUT.tuners_guide: Lowering ACOUT to approximately 90 to 100 counts (~1.8 to 2.0 Volts above MINTHR / ~50% throttle) disengages the A/C compressor earlier during moderate acceleration. This gives the vehicle a more responsive and energetic feel during highway passing maneuvers without needing to floor the pedal. Raising ACOUT toward 180 counts delays compressor cutout until near 90% throttle, which keeps cabin cooling active during spirited mid-throttle driving. Setting ACOUT to maximum (255 counts) disables wide-open throttle A/C cutout entirely.
ACOUT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Mid-Throttle Passing Response**: * Lower `ACOUT` to 90 to 100 counts (~50% throttle) to drop compressor drag during moderate passing maneuvers.
* **Sustained Cabin Cooling**: * Raise `ACOUT` to 160 to 180 counts to maintain air conditioning during moderately aggressive mountain driving.
* **Disabling Wide-Open Cutout**: * Set `ACOUT` to 255 counts to keep the A/C clutch engaged across all throttle angles.
ACOUT.operating_conditions:
Takes effect during heavy or wide-open throttle acceleration, immediately disengaging the A/C compressor clutch to eliminate accessory drag and maximize engine power.

ACCRPM.overview: ACCRPM defines the maximum engine speed lockout threshold for air conditioning compressor clutch engagement. Automotive reciprocating piston and rotary vane air conditioning compressors are engineered with strict rotational speed limits. Spinning an automotive A/C compressor beyond 4500 to 5000 engine RPM generates severe internal friction, reed valve flutter, excessive head pressure, and clutch bearing failure. In factory calibrations, ACCRPM is configured to 4000 RPM (32000 counts in 16-bit word format). If engine speed exceeds 4000 RPM, the controller prevents the A/C clutch from engaging, protecting the mechanical compressor and accessory drive belt during high-RPM driving.

Automotive reciprocating piston and rotary vane air conditioning compressors are engineered with strict rotational speed limits. Spinning an automotive A/C compressor beyond 4500 to 5000 engine RPM generates severe internal friction, reed valve flutter, excessive head pressure, and clutch bearing failure. In factory calibrations, `ACCRPM` is configured to 4000 RPM (32000 counts in 16-bit word format). If engine speed exceeds 4000 RPM, the controller prevents the A/C clutch from engaging, protecting the mechanical compressor and accessory drive belt during high-RPM driving.
ACCRPM.tuners_guide: Never raise ACCRPM above 4500 RPM. On modified turbocharged engines built for high engine speeds (6000 to 7000+ RPM), ACCRPM provides essential mechanical protection for the compressor clutch and accessory drive belt. Lowering ACCRPM to 3500 RPM reduces mechanical strain on aged factory compressors during highway driving. Setting ACCRPM too low (under 3000 RPM) leads to loss of cabin air conditioning during normal highway cruising in vehicles with high-RPM final drive gearing.
ACCRPM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Compressor Protection Ceiling**: * Never calibrate `ACCRPM` above 4500 RPM to protect internal reed valves and clutch bearings.
* **High-RPM Track Safety**: * Ensures the compressor is locked out when racing or revving through the gears.
* **Highway Gearing Considerations**: * Keep `ACCRPM` at least 500 RPM above normal 70 MPH highway cruising engine speed to maintain cabin cooling.
ACCRPM.operating_conditions:
Takes effect whenever engine speed exceeds 4,000 RPM with the air conditioning on, immediately disengaging the compressor clutch to protect against high-RPM mechanical damage.

ACCTIM.overview: ACCTIM defines the post-start time delay enforced after the engine transitions into run mode before the controller allows the air conditioning compressor clutch to engage. When starting an engine with the climate control switch left in the ON position, immediately engaging the compressor clutch while the starter motor is cranking or disengaging would place severe mechanical drag on the starter drive, battery voltage, and cold engine combustion. In factory calibrations, ACCTIM is set to 4 counts, representing approximately 0.4 seconds. This holds the A/C clutch disengaged until the engine has cleanly established oil pressure and stable idle flare control.
ACCTIM.overview_markdown: `ACCTIM` defines the post-start time delay enforced after the engine transitions into run mode before the controller allows the air conditioning compressor clutch to engage. When starting an engine with the climate control switch left in the ON position, immediately engaging the compressor clutch while the starter motor is cranking or disengaging would place severe mechanical drag on the starter drive, battery voltage, and cold engine combustion. In factory calibrations, `ACCTIM` is set to 4 counts, representing approximately 0.4 seconds. This holds the A/C clutch disengaged until the engine has cleanly established oil pressure and stable idle flare control.
ACCTIM.tuners_guide: Raising ACCTIM to 1.0 or 2.0 seconds (10 to 20 counts) gives modified engines with large fuel injectors, lightweight flywheels, or low-vacuum camshafts extra time to settle into a stable idle after starting before absorbing compressor load. This eliminates startup stumbling or immediate stalling when turning the key with the A/C on in hot weather. Lowering ACCTIM reduces the startup delay, but setting it to zero engages the compressor clutch during starter disengagement, creating harsh starter gear shock.
ACCTIM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Startup Idle Settling**: * Increase `ACCTIM` to 1.0 to 2.0 seconds (10 to 20 counts) on performance engines to allow idle flare to settle smoothly.
* **Starter Motor Protection**: * Prevents heavy mechanical cranking drag when starting with the dashboard A/C button depressed.
* **Zeroing Caution**: * Do not set `ACCTIM` to zero to avoid engaging the compressor clutch while oil pressure is still building.
ACCTIM.operating_conditions:
